title: Mapping Antibiotic-Use Pathways and Leverage Points for AMR Control in Kinshasa’s Pig and Poultry Systems: A One Health Stakeholder Analysis
content: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global public health threat, particularly in low  and middle income countries where fragmented regulatory frameworks foster inappropriate practices and therapeutic failures. This study was conducted in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo, to examine access to and use of antibiotics in pig and poultry farming, and to analyze stakeholder perceptions of their roles and responsibilities in AMR governance. Data were collected through 149 in depth interviews and six focus groups involving medical doctors, veterinarians, paraprofessionals, farmers, drug sellers, laboratory technicians, regulatory agents, and technical partners. Respondents confirmed frequent use of antibiotics for prevention and treatment of infections, but also as growth promoters, notably colistin. Therapeutic failures were commonly reported, leading to empirical switching of antibiotics without susceptibility testing. Farmers mainly obtained antibiotics from veterinarians, while veterinarians themselves sometimes relied on human pharmacies due to limited availability of veterinary drugs. Medical doctors, in contrast, prescribed antibiotics exclusively through formal channels. Stakeholders emphasized weak veterinary services, lack of market control, and limited involvement of policymakers. Relational mapping revealed critical gaps in intersectoral information flows, highlighting the need for improved coordination. Overall, the findings suggest that combating AMR in pig and poultry farms in the city of Kinshasa requires an integrated One Health approach, including stronger governance of antibiotic supply chains, reduction of infectious pressure through prevention and biosecurity, improvement of therapeutic decision making, and institutionalization of coordination mechanisms.
